name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q01 - Aristotle early scientific classification basis

questiontext.text: Who was the earliest to attempt a more scientific basis for classification by dividing plants into trees, shrubs, and herbs, and animals into those with red blood and those without?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Early attempts at biological classification evolved from instinctive, utilitarian groupings (for food, shelter, and clothing) to morphological criteria.

Step 2: Evaluation
Aristotle used simple morphological characters to classify plants into trees, shrubs, and herbs, and divided animals into two groups based on whether they had red blood or not.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, Aristotle was the earliest to attempt a more scientific basis for classification using these criteria.

answer.text: Aristotle
Linnaeus
R.H. Whittaker
Dmitri Ivanowsky

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q02 - Limitations of Linnaeus Two Kingdom system

questiontext.text: Which of the following distinctions was not made by Linnaeus' Two Kingdom system of classification?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Linnaeus' Two Kingdom system grouped all organisms into Plantae and Animalia based largely on gross morphology and presence of a cell wall.

Step 2: Evaluation
This system failed to distinguish between eukaryotes and prokaryotes, unicellular and multicellular organisms, and photosynthetic (green algae) and non-photosynthetic (fungi) organisms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the Two Kingdom system did not distinguish between eukaryotes and prokaryotes (nor between unicellular/multicellular or photosynthetic/non-photosynthetic organisms).

answer.text: Plants and animals based on gross morphology
Eukaryotes and prokaryotes, unicellular and multicellular organisms, and photosynthetic and non-photosynthetic organisms
Trees, shrubs, and herbs among terrestrial plants
Organisms with red blood and those without red blood

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q03 - Main criteria of Whittaker Five Kingdom classification

questiontext.text: Which set of main criteria was used by R.H. Whittaker (1969) to propose the Five Kingdom Classification?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
R.H. Whittaker (1969) proposed the Five Kingdom Classification comprising Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia.

Step 2: Evaluation
The main criteria used by Whittaker were cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction, and phylogenetic relationships. Criteria such as presence of red blood or exclusively gross morphology belong to earlier systems.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction, and phylogenetic relationships constitute Whittaker's main classification criteria.

answer.text: Presence of red blood, habitat, and stem height
Gross morphology, economic utility, and locomotion only
Cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction, and phylogenetic relationships
Presence of chlorophyll, blood colour, and number of flagella

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q04 - Three-domain system and six kingdom classification

questiontext.text: How does the three-domain system lead to a six-kingdom classification?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Beyond the Five Kingdom Classification, a three-domain system was proposed to reflect deeper evolutionary divisions among prokaryotes.

Step 2: Evaluation
The three-domain system divides Kingdom Monera into two separate domains while placing all remaining eukaryotic kingdoms (Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia) in the third domain, thereby creating a six-kingdom classification.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, dividing Kingdom Monera into two domains and keeping the remaining eukaryotic kingdoms in the third domain yields a six-kingdom classification.

answer.text: It divides Kingdom Protista into two domains and merges Monera with Fungi
It places viruses and viroids into a separate sixth kingdom
It splits Kingdom Plantae into algae and embryophytes as separate domains
It divides Kingdom Monera into two domains, leaving the remaining eukaryotic kingdoms in the third domain

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q05 - Separation of Fungi from Plantae

questiontext.text: In earlier classification systems, bacteria, blue-green algae, fungi, mosses, ferns, gymnosperms, and angiosperms were all placed under 'Plants'. What single unifying character grouped them together, and why were fungi later placed in a separate kingdom?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Earlier systems relied on broad structural features, whereas modern classification considers cell wall chemistry and mode of nutrition.

Step 2: Evaluation
All organisms included under 'Plants' in earlier systems shared the presence of a cell wall in their cells. However, fungi are heterotrophic and possess chitin in their cell walls, whereas green plants are autotrophic with a cellulosic cell wall.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the unifying character was the presence of a cell wall, and fungi were separated because they are heterotrophic and have chitinous cell walls.

answer.text: Presence of a cell wall; fungi were separated because they are heterotrophic and have chitin in their walls instead of cellulose
Presence of chlorophyll; fungi were separated because they are prokaryotic
Absence of nuclear membrane; fungi were separated because they are unicellular
Presence of flagella; fungi were separated because they lack a cell wall

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q06 - Reclassification of unicellular eukaryotes into Protista

questiontext.text: Kingdom Protista has brought together Chlamydomonas and Chlorella with Paramoecium and Amoeba. Where were these organisms placed in earlier classification systems?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Changing classification criteria led to regrouping all unicellular eukaryotic organisms under Kingdom Protista.

Step 2: Evaluation
Chlamydomonas and Chlorella (which have cell walls) were earlier placed in Algae within Plants, whereas Paramoecium and Amoeba (which lack cell walls) were earlier placed in the animal kingdom.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, Chlamydomonas and Chlorella were earlier placed in Plants (Algae), while Paramoecium and Amoeba were placed in Animalia.

answer.text: All four were earlier placed in Kingdom Monera
Chlamydomonas and Chlorella were in Plants (Algae), while Paramoecium and Amoeba were in Animalia
Chlamydomonas and Paramoecium were in Plants, while Chlorella and Amoeba were in Fungi
All four were earlier placed in Kingdom Fungi

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q07 - Comparative characteristics of the Five Kingdoms

questiontext.text: According to Whittaker's Five Kingdom Classification, which of the following statements accurately compares the cellular and organisational characteristics across kingdoms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The five kingdoms differ systematically in cell type, cell wall, nuclear membrane, body organisation, and mode of nutrition.

Step 2: Evaluation
1. Nuclear membrane is absent in Monera (prokaryotic) and present in Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia (eukaryotic).
2. Body organisation is cellular in both Monera and Protista, whereas Fungi show multicellular/loose tissue organisation, Plantae show tissue/organ organisation, and Animalia show tissue/organ/organ system organisation.
3. Cell wall is absent in Animalia, present in some Protista, noncellulosic in Monera, chitinous in Fungi, and cellulosic in Plantae.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, nuclear membrane is absent only in Monera, and body organisation is cellular in both Monera and Protista.

answer.text: Nuclear membrane is absent in both Monera and Protista
Cell wall is present in all members of Protista and Fungi
Nuclear membrane is absent only in Monera, and body organisation is cellular in both Monera and Protista
Body organisation in Fungi is strictly at the organ-system level

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q08 - Meaning of phylogenetic classification system

questiontext.text: What is meant by a classification system being phylogenetic?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Over time, biologists have attempted to evolve a classification system that goes beyond superficial similarities.

Step 2: Evaluation
A phylogenetic classification system reflects not only morphological, physiological, and reproductive similarities, but is also based on evolutionary relationships among organisms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, a phylogenetic classification system is one based on evolutionary relationships.

answer.text: It is based solely on external morphological characters
It classifies organisms strictly by their economic usefulness to humans
It groups organisms exclusively according to their habitat
It is based on evolutionary relationships in addition to morphological, physiological, and reproductive similarities

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q09 - Four morphological categories of bacteria

questiontext.text: Bacteria, the sole members of Kingdom Monera, are grouped into four categories based on their shape. Which of the following correctly pairs the shape with the bacterial category?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bacteria are classified morphologically into four shape-based categories: coccus, bacillus, vibrium, and spirillum.

Step 2: Evaluation
Coccus is spherical, Bacillus is rod-shaped, Vibrium is comma-shaped, and Spirillum is spiral-shaped.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, spherical is Coccus, rod-shaped is Bacillus, comma-shaped is Vibrium, and spiral is Spirillum.

answer.text: Spherical – Coccus; Rod-shaped – Bacillus; Comma-shaped – Vibrium; Spiral – Spirillum
Spherical – Bacillus; Rod-shaped – Coccus; Comma-shaped – Spirillum; Spiral – Vibrium
Spherical – Vibrium; Rod-shaped – Spirillum; Comma-shaped – Coccus; Spiral – Bacillus
Spherical – Coccus; Rod-shaped – Vibrium; Comma-shaped – Bacillus; Spiral – Spirillum

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q10 - Metabolic diversity of bacteria

questiontext.text: Compared to many other organisms, bacteria as a group show the most extensive metabolic diversity. What is the mode of nutrition of the vast majority of bacteria?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Although bacterial structure is very simple, bacteria are complex in behaviour and exhibit extensive metabolic diversity.

Step 2: Evaluation
Some bacteria are photosynthetic autotrophs or chemosynthetic autotrophs, but the vast majority of bacteria are heterotrophs that depend on other organisms or dead organic matter for food.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the vast majority of bacteria are heterotrophs.

answer.text: Photosynthetic autotrophs
Heterotrophs
Chemosynthetic autotrophs
Holozoic ingestors

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q11 - Reason for archaebacteria survival in extreme habitats

questiontext.text: Archaebacteria such as halophiles, thermoacidophiles, and methanogens survive in some of the most harsh habitats. Which feature is responsible for their survival in extreme conditions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Archaebacteria inhabit extreme salty areas (halophiles), hot springs (thermoacidophiles), and marshy areas (methanogens).

Step 2: Evaluation
They differ from other bacteria in having a different cell wall structure, and this feature is responsible for their survival in extreme conditions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, a different cell wall structure enables archaebacteria to survive in extreme habitats.

answer.text: Presence of a well-defined nuclear membrane
Presence of chlorophyll a inside chloroplasts
Having a different cell wall structure from other bacteria
Complete absence of a cell wall

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q12 - Role of methanogens in ruminant animals

questiontext.text: Methanogens are present in the gut of several ruminant animals such as cows and buffaloes. What is their primary role there?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Methanogens are a group of archaebacteria that thrive in anaerobic marshy habitats and animal guts.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the gut of ruminant animals such as cows and buffaloes, methanogens are responsible for the production of methane (biogas) from the dung of these animals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, methanogens produce methane (biogas) from the dung of ruminant animals.

answer.text: Fixation of atmospheric nitrogen in root nodules
Oxidation of ammonia to nitrates for ATP production
Production of antibiotics to protect the host gut
Production of methane (biogas) from the dung of these animals

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q13 - Characteristics of cyanobacteria

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements accurately describes cyanobacteria (blue-green algae)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic autotrophic eubacteria.

Step 2: Evaluation
They have chlorophyll a similar to green plants, can be unicellular, colonial, or filamentous (freshwater, marine, or terrestrial), have colonies generally surrounded by a gelatinous sheath, and often form blooms in polluted water bodies.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, cyanobacteria have chlorophyll a, form colonies surrounded by a gelatinous sheath, and often cause blooms in polluted water bodies.

answer.text: They have chlorophyll a similar to green plants, form colonies with a gelatinous sheath, and often form blooms in polluted water bodies
They are eukaryotic organisms with chitinous cell walls and lack photosynthetic pigments
They are exclusively marine and cause red tides through rapid multiplication
They lack a cell wall and are the smallest living cells known

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q14 - Nitrogen fixation in heterocysts

questiontext.text: Specialised cells called heterocysts, which fix atmospheric nitrogen, are found in which pair of cyanobacteria?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain filamentous cyanobacteria differentiate specialised cells for nitrogen fixation.

Step 2: Evaluation
Nostoc and Anabaena can fix atmospheric nitrogen in specialised cells called heterocysts. In contrast, Spirogyra and Chlamydomonas are eukaryotic algae, and Mucor and Rhizopus are fungi.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, heterocysts for atmospheric nitrogen fixation are found in Nostoc and Anabaena.

answer.text: Spirogyra and Chlamydomonas
Nostoc and Anabaena
Mucor and Rhizopus
Gonyaulax and Euglena

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q15 - Chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria and nutrient recycling

questiontext.text: How do chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria obtain energy for ATP production, and what major ecological role do they play?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chemosynthetic autotrophs synthesise food without sunlight by using chemical energy from inorganic oxidations.

Step 2: Evaluation
Chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria oxidise various inorganic substances such as nitrates, nitrites, and ammonia and use the released energy for ATP production. They play a great role in recycling nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorous, iron, and sulphur.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, they oxidise inorganic substances such as nitrates, nitrites, and ammonia for ATP production and recycle nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorous, iron, and sulphur.

answer.text: They trap sunlight using chlorophyll a; they cause red tides in oceans
They ingest dead organic matter; they produce biogas in ruminant guts
They oxidise inorganic substances like nitrates, nitrites, and ammonia; they recycle nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorous, iron, and sulphur
They ferment milk sugar; they are used to make bread and beer

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q16 - Beneficial and pathogenic roles of heterotrophic bacteria

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets consists entirely of diseases caused by different bacteria?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
While the majority of heterotrophic bacteria are important decomposers and many are useful (making curd, producing antibiotics, fixing nitrogen in legume roots), some are pathogens.

Step 2: Evaluation
Cholera, typhoid, tetanus, and citrus canker are well-known diseases caused by bacteria. In contrast, malaria is caused by a sporozoan protozoan (Plasmodium), sleeping sickness by Trypanosoma, wheat rust by Puccinia (a fungus), and mumps/influenza/AIDS by viruses.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, and citrus canker are all bacterial diseases.

answer.text: Cholera, malaria, tetanus, and mumps
Typhoid, wheat rust, sleeping sickness, and AIDS
Citrus canker, potato spindle tuber, influenza, and cholera
Cholera, typhoid, tetanus, and citrus canker

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q17 - Modes of reproduction in bacteria

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately summarises reproduction in bacteria?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bacteria exhibit simple asexual division as well as survival and genetic exchange mechanisms.

Step 2: Evaluation
Bacteria reproduce mainly by fission. Under unfavourable conditions, they produce spores. They also reproduce by a sort of sexual reproduction by adopting a primitive type of DNA transfer from one bacterium to another.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, bacteria reproduce mainly by fission, form spores under unfavourable conditions, and show a primitive type of DNA transfer.

answer.text: They reproduce mainly by fission, produce spores under unfavourable conditions, and show a primitive type of DNA transfer
They reproduce exclusively by budding and never form spores
They undergo typical eukaryotic mitosis and meiosis with gamete fusion
They reproduce only by exogenous conidia formed on conidiophores

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q18 - Characteristics of Mycoplasma

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a distinguishing set of features of Mycoplasma?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mycoplasma represents an exceptional group within Kingdom Monera.

Step 2: Evaluation
Mycoplasma are organisms that completely lack a cell wall, are the smallest living cells known, can survive without oxygen, and many are pathogenic in animals and plants.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, Mycoplasma completely lack a cell wall, are the smallest living cells known, and can survive without oxygen.

answer.text: Rigid cellulosic cell wall, obligate aerobes, and non-pathogenic
Complete lack of a cell wall, smallest living cells known, and ability to survive without oxygen
Silica-embedded cell wall, largest eukaryotic cells, and photosynthetic
Chitinous cell wall, filamentous hyphae, and obligate parasites only in fungi

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q19 - General characteristics of Kingdom Protista

questiontext.text: Which statement is true regarding Kingdom Protista?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kingdom Protista serves as a link between plants, animals, and fungi.

Step 2: Evaluation
All single-celled eukaryotes are placed under Protista, though its boundaries are not well defined. Members are primarily aquatic, contain a well-defined nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles, and reproduce both asexually and sexually by cell fusion and zygote formation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, all single-celled eukaryotes are placed under Protista, and their cells contain a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

answer.text: All members are multicellular prokaryotes lacking a nuclear membrane
Its boundaries are strictly defined and all members are exclusively terrestrial
It includes all single-celled eukaryotes with a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, and members are primarily aquatic
Members reproduce exclusively by asexual fission and never form zygotes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q20 - Chrysophytes and chief producers in oceans

questiontext.text: Which group of protists includes diatoms and golden algae (desmids), floats passively in water currents as plankton, and includes the chief 'producers' in the oceans?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Within Kingdom Protista, different groups occupy distinct ecological niches in freshwater and marine ecosystems.

Step 2: Evaluation
Chrysophytes include diatoms and golden algae (desmids). They are microscopic, float passively in water currents (plankton), are mostly photosynthetic, and diatoms are the chief 'producers' in the oceans.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, Chrysophytes is the group that includes diatoms and desmids and serves as the chief oceanic producers.

answer.text: Dinoflagellates
Euglenoids
Slime moulds
Chrysophytes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q21 - Diatom cell walls and diatomaceous earth

questiontext.text: Why are the cell walls of diatoms indestructible, leading to the accumulation of 'diatomaceous earth', and what is this gritty soil used for?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Diatoms possess a unique cell wall architecture that resists decomposition over geological timescales.

Step 2: Evaluation
In diatoms, the cell walls form two thin overlapping shells that fit together as in a soap box, and the walls are embedded with silica, making them indestructible. Their accumulation over billions of years forms gritty 'diatomaceous earth', which is used in polishing and filtration of oils and syrups.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, silica-embedded overlapping shells make diatom walls indestructible, and diatomaceous earth is used in polishing and filtration of oils and syrups.

answer.text: The walls are embedded with silica; used in polishing and filtration of oils and syrups
The walls are made of chitin; used in making bread and beer
The walls are made of stiff cellulose plates; used in biogas production
The walls are composed of proteinaceous pellicle; used in antibiotic synthesis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q22 - Cell wall and flagellar arrangement in dinoflagellates

questiontext.text: Which combination of cell wall and flagellar arrangement is characteristic of dinoflagellates?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dinoflagellates are mostly marine, photosynthetic protists with distinctive surface armour and flagellar orientation.

Step 2: Evaluation
Their cell wall has stiff cellulose plates on the outer surface, and most of them have two flagella—one lying longitudinally and the other transversely in a furrow between the wall plates.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, stiff cellulose plates on the outer surface and two flagella (one longitudinal, one transverse in a furrow) characterise dinoflagellates.

answer.text: Silica-embedded overlapping shells; flagella absent
Stiff cellulose plates on the outer surface; two flagella, one longitudinal and one transverse in a furrow
Flexible protein-rich pellicle; two unequal anterior flagella
Chitinous wall; thousands of coordinated cilia

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q23 - Red tides caused by Gonyaulax

questiontext.text: Rapid multiplication of which organism makes the sea appear red ('red tides') and releases toxins that may kill marine animals such as fishes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain marine dinoflagellates undergo population explosions that discolour seawater and harm marine fauna.

Step 2: Evaluation
Red dinoflagellates such as Gonyaulax undergo rapid multiplication, making the sea appear red (red tides), and the toxins released by such large numbers may kill marine animals like fishes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, Gonyaulax is responsible for red tides and toxin-mediated fish mortality.

answer.text: Nostoc
Trypanosoma
Gonyaulax
Euglena

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q24 - Pellicle and flagella in Euglenoids

questiontext.text: Instead of a cell wall, euglenoids possess a protein-rich layer that makes their body flexible. What is this layer called, and where are most euglenoids found?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Euglenoids lack a rigid cell wall and instead have a flexible outer proteinaceous covering.

Step 2: Evaluation
Majority of euglenoids are freshwater organisms found in stagnant water, and they possess a protein-rich layer called pellicle that makes their body flexible, along with two flagella (one short and one long).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the layer is called pellicle, and most euglenoids are found in stagnant freshwater.

answer.text: Capsid; deep marine oceans
Mucilagenous sheath; hot springs
Mycelium; decaying wood
Pellicle; stagnant freshwater

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q25 - Mixotrophic nutrition and pigments in Euglenoids

questiontext.text: How do euglenoids behave nutritionally when deprived of sunlight, and how do their photosynthetic pigments compare to higher plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Euglenoids show dual nutritional behaviour depending on light availability and share pigment similarities with higher plants.

Step 2: Evaluation
Though photosynthetic in the presence of sunlight, euglenoids behave like heterotrophs by predating on other smaller organisms when deprived of sunlight. Moreover, their pigments are identical to those present in higher plants.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, in the absence of sunlight they behave as heterotrophs by predating on smaller organisms, and their pigments are identical to those of higher plants.

answer.text: They behave as heterotrophs by predating on smaller organisms; their pigments are identical to those of higher plants
They switch to chemosynthesis by oxidising ammonia; their pigments are unique to bacteria
They form resistant spores immediately; they completely lack photosynthetic pigments
They become obligate parasites on plants; their pigments are identical to fungi

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q26 - Slime moulds plasmodium and spore formation

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately describes the life cycle of slime moulds under suitable versus unfavourable conditions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Slime moulds are saprophytic protists whose developmental state responds to environmental conditions.

Step 2: Evaluation
Under suitable conditions, slime moulds form an aggregation called a plasmodium that may grow and spread over several feet. During unfavourable conditions, the plasmodium differentiates to form fruiting bodies bearing spores at their tips. These spores possess true walls, are extremely resistant, survive for many years, and are dispersed by air currents.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, they form a plasmodium under suitable conditions and differentiate into fruiting bodies with true-walled, air-dispersed spores during unfavourable conditions.

answer.text: They form fruiting bodies under suitable conditions and aggregate into a plasmodium during unfavourable conditions
They form a plasmodium under suitable conditions and differentiate into fruiting bodies bearing true-walled, air-dispersed spores during unfavourable conditions
Their spores lack cell walls and are dispersed exclusively by water currents
They are photosynthetic protists that form diatomaceous earth upon death

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q27 - Amoeboid and flagellated protozoans

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about amoeboid and flagellated protozoans is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Protozoans are heterotrophic protists (predators or parasites) divided into four major groups.

Step 2: Evaluation
Amoeboid protozoans move and capture prey by putting out pseudopodia (as in Amoeba), marine forms have silica shells on their surface, and Entamoeba is a parasitic form. Flagellated protozoans are free-living or parasitic, and parasitic forms such as Trypanosoma cause sleeping sickness.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, marine amoeboid protozoans have silica shells on their surface, Entamoeba is a parasitic amoeboid protozoan, and Trypanosoma is a flagellated protozoan causing sleeping sickness.

answer.text: Freshwater amoeboid protozoans have silica shells, whereas marine forms lack any surface covering
Trypanosoma is an amoeboid protozoan that causes malaria using pseudopodia
Marine amoeboid protozoans have silica shells, Entamoeba is parasitic, and the flagellated protozoan Trypanosoma causes sleeping sickness
All flagellated protozoans are exclusively free-living and photosynthetic

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q28 - Ciliated protozoans and sporozoans

questiontext.text: How do ciliated protozoans like Paramoecium obtain food, and what characterises sporozoans like Plasmodium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ciliated protozoans and sporozoans represent specialised predatory and parasitic adaptations within Protozoa.

Step 2: Evaluation
Ciliated protozoans have thousands of cilia whose coordinated movement steers food-laden water into a cavity (gullet) opening to the outside of the cell surface. Sporozoans include diverse organisms that have an infectious spore-like stage in their life cycle, such as Plasmodium (malarial parasite).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, coordinated movement of cilia steers food-laden water into the gullet in Paramoecium, while sporozoans possess an infectious spore-like stage in their life cycle.

answer.text: Paramoecium uses pseudopodia to engulf food; Plasmodium uses two unequal flagella
Paramoecium photosynthesises in sunlight; Plasmodium is a saprophyte on decaying leaves
Paramoecium absorbs nutrients via hyphae; Plasmodium lacks any spore-like stage
Coordinated movement of cilia steers food-laden water into a gullet in Paramoecium; sporozoans have an infectious spore-like stage in their life cycle

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q29 - Fungal hyphae, mycelium, and cell wall

questiontext.text: With the exception of unicellular yeasts, fungi are filamentous. What are continuous tubular hyphae filled with multinucleated cytoplasm called, and what are fungal cell walls composed of?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Fungal bodies consist of slender thread-like hyphae forming a network called mycelium.

Step 2: Evaluation
Hyphae that are continuous tubes filled with multinucleated cytoplasm are called coenocytic hyphae. The cell walls of fungi are composed of chitin and polysaccharides.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, such hyphae are called coenocytic hyphae, and fungal cell walls are composed of chitin and polysaccharides.

answer.text: Coenocytic hyphae; chitin and polysaccharides
Septate hyphae; cellulose and pectin
Conidiophores; silica and lignin
Plasmodium; peptidoglycan and amino acids

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q30 - Symbiotic associations of fungi

questiontext.text: Fungi can live as symbionts in association with algae and with roots of higher plants. What are these two symbiotic associations called, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Besides saprophytic and parasitic modes, many fungi form mutually beneficial symbiotic associations.

Step 2: Evaluation
Fungi living in association with algae are called lichens, and fungi living in association with roots of higher plants are called mycorrhiza.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the associations are called lichens and mycorrhiza, respectively.

answer.text: Mycorrhiza and lichens
Lichens and mycorrhiza
Ascocarps and basidiocarps
Heterocysts and plasmodia

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q31 - Vegetative, asexual, and sexual spores in fungi

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly classifies the spores involved in asexual versus sexual reproduction in fungi?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Fungi reproduce vegetatively (fragmentation, fission, budding), asexually, and sexually via distinct types of spores.

Step 2: Evaluation
Asexual reproduction in fungi occurs by conidia, sporangiospores, or zoospores. Sexual reproduction occurs by oospores, ascospores, and basidiospores, produced in distinct structures called fruiting bodies.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, asexual spores are conidia, sporangiospores, or zoospores, while sexual spores are oospores, ascospores, and basidiospores.

answer.text: Asexual: oospores, ascospores, basidiospores; Sexual: conidia, sporangiospores, zoospores
Asexual: ascospores and zoospores; Sexual: conidia and basidiospores
Asexual: conidia, sporangiospores, or zoospores; Sexual: oospores, ascospores, and basidiospores
Asexual: fragmentation and budding; Sexual: sporangiospores and conidia

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q32 - Dikaryophase in Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes

questiontext.text: In ascomycetes and basidiomycetes, fusion of two haploid cells does not immediately result in a diploid (\(2n\)) cell. Instead, an intervening stage with two nuclei per cell occurs. What are this condition and phase called?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During fungal sexual reproduction, plasmogamy is followed by karyogamy, either immediately or after an intervening binucleate stage.

Step 2: Evaluation
In ascomycetes and basidiomycetes, an intervening dikaryotic stage (\(n + n\), two nuclei per cell) occurs between plasmogamy and karyogamy. This condition is called a dikaryon, and the phase is called the dikaryophase of the fungus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the condition is called a dikaryon (\(n + n\)) and the phase is called dikaryophase.

answer.text: Coenocyte and coenocytic phase
Plasmodium and sporophytic phase
Zygospore and gametophytic phase
Dikaryon and dikaryophase

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q33 - Characteristics and examples of Phycomycetes

questiontext.text: Which of the following features and examples belong to class Phycomycetes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phycomycetes are lower fungi found in aquatic habitats, on decaying wood in moist/damp places, or as obligate parasites on plants.

Step 2: Evaluation
Their mycelium is aseptate and coenocytic. Asexual reproduction takes place by motile zoospores or non-motile aplanospores produced endogenously in a sporangium. A zygospore forms by gamete fusion. Common examples are Mucor, Rhizopus (bread mould), and Albugo (parasitic fungus on mustard).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, aseptate coenocytic mycelium, endogenous zoospores/aplanospores, and examples Mucor, Rhizopus, and Albugo characterise Phycomycetes.

answer.text: Aseptate, coenocytic mycelium; endogenous zoospores or aplanospores; Mucor, Rhizopus, and Albugo
Branched, septate mycelium; exogenous conidia on conidiophores; Aspergillus and Claviceps
Branched, septate mycelium; exogenous basidiospores; Agaricus and Ustilago
Septate mycelium; sexual stage absent; Alternaria and Trichoderma

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q34 - Ascomycetes general features and conidia

questiontext.text: Members of Ascomycetes (sac-fungi) are mostly multicellular (like Penicillium) or rarely unicellular (like yeast, Saccharomyces). How are their asexual spores produced?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ascomycetes possess a branched and septate mycelium and exhibit distinct exogenous asexual and endogenous sexual spore formation.

Step 2: Evaluation
In Ascomycetes, the asexual spores are conidia produced exogenously on special mycelium called conidiophores. On germination, conidia produce new mycelium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, asexual spores in Ascomycetes are conidia produced exogenously on conidiophores.

answer.text: Endogenously inside sporangia as motile zoospores
Exogenously as conidia on special mycelium called conidiophores
Exogenously as basidiospores on club-shaped basidia
Endogenously as ascospores inside ascocarps

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q35 - Ascomycetes sexual spores, Neurospora, and edible delicacies

questiontext.text: Which ascomycete is used extensively in biochemical and genetic work, and which edible members of Ascomycetes are considered delicacies?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ascomycetes include organisms of major scientific and culinary importance, producing endogenous ascospores in sac-like asci arranged in ascocarps.

Step 2: Evaluation
Neurospora is used extensively in biochemical and genetic work. Many members like morels and truffles are edible and are considered delicacies. In contrast, Agaricus is a basidiomycete, and Ustilago and Puccinia are parasitic basidiomycetes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, Neurospora is used in biochemical and genetic work, and morels and truffles are edible delicacies.

answer.text: Aspergillus; rusts and smuts
Claviceps; Mucor and Rhizopus
Neurospora; morels and truffles
Penicillium; Ustilago and Puccinia

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q36 - Reproduction in Basidiomycetes without sex organs

questiontext.text: In Basidiomycetes, asexual spores are generally not found and sex organs are absent. How is plasmogamy brought about in this class?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Basidiomycetes (mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs) have a branched, septate mycelium and commonly reproduce vegetatively by fragmentation.

Step 2: Evaluation
Although sex organs are absent, plasmogamy is brought about by fusion of two vegetative or somatic cells of different strains or genotypes. The resultant structure is dikaryotic, which ultimately gives rise to a basidium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, plasmogamy occurs by fusion of two vegetative or somatic cells of different strains or genotypes.

answer.text: By fusion of two motile zoospores inside a sporangium
By germination of exogenous conidia on conidiophores
By direct conjugation of male and female gametangia
By fusion of two vegetative or somatic cells of different strains or genotypes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q37 - Basidiospore formation and examples of Basidiomycetes

questiontext.text: Where do karyogamy and meiosis take place in Basidiomycetes, how are the resulting basidiospores borne, and which trio represents members of this class?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Following dikaryon formation in Basidiomycetes, nuclear fusion and reduction division are localised to the basidium.

Step 2: Evaluation
Karyogamy and meiosis take place in the basidium, producing four basidiospores. These basidiospores are exogenously produced on the basidium, and basidia are arranged in fruiting bodies called basidiocarps. Common members are Agaricus (mushroom), Ustilago (smut), and Puccinia (rust fungus).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, karyogamy and meiosis occur in the basidium, producing four exogenous basidiospores, with examples Agaricus, Ustilago, and Puccinia.

answer.text: In the basidium; four basidiospores produced exogenously; Agaricus, Ustilago, and Puccinia
In the ascus; eight ascospores produced endogenously; Aspergillus, Claviceps, and Neurospora
In the sporangium; zoospores produced endogenously; Mucor, Rhizopus, and Albugo
In the conidiophore; conidia produced exogenously; Alternaria, Colletotrichum, and Trichoderma

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q38 - Deuteromycetes as imperfect fungi

questiontext.text: Why are Deuteromycetes commonly known as 'imperfect fungi', and what happens when their sexual stages are discovered?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Deuteromycetes is a provisional grouping of fungi whose sexual life cycles have not yet been observed.

Step 2: Evaluation
They are called imperfect fungi because only their asexual or vegetative phases are known (reproducing only by conidia, with a septate and branched mycelium). Once their perfect (sexual) stages are discovered, they are moved out of Deuteromycetes into the classes they rightly belong to—often Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, only their asexual or vegetative phases are known, and once sexual stages are discovered they are moved to classes such as Ascomycetes or Basidiomycetes.

answer.text: They lack a cell wall; once discovered, they are moved to Kingdom Protista
Only their asexual or vegetative phases are known; once sexual stages are discovered, they are often moved to Ascomycetes or Basidiomycetes
They have aseptate coenocytic hyphae; once sexual stages are discovered, they are moved to Phycomycetes
They reproduce exclusively by sexual ascospores; they remain permanently in Deuteromycetes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q39 - Partially heterotrophic plants in Kingdom Plantae

questiontext.text: While most members of Kingdom Plantae are autotrophic, a few are partially heterotrophic. Which of the following correctly identifies insectivorous and parasitic plant examples, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kingdom Plantae includes eukaryotic chlorophyll-containing organisms with cellulosic cell walls, though a few exhibit partial heterotrophy.

Step 2: Evaluation
Bladderwort and Venus fly trap are examples of insectivorous plants, whereas Cuscuta is a parasitic plant.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, Bladderwort and Venus fly trap are insectivorous plants, and Cuscuta is a parasite.

answer.text: Cuscuta; Bladderwort and Venus fly trap
Albugo; Puccinia and Ustilago
Bladderwort and Venus fly trap; Cuscuta
Nostoc and Anabaena; Chlamydomonas

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q40 - Alternation of generation in Kingdom Plantae

questiontext.text: What is the phenomenon of alternation of generation in the life cycle of plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plant life cycles involve two distinct multicellular phases with different ploidy levels.

Step 2: Evaluation
In plants, the diploid sporophytic phase and the haploid gametophytic phase alternate with each other. The lengths of these phases and whether they are free-living or dependent on others vary among different plant groups.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, alternation of generation refers to the alternation between the diploid sporophytic and haploid gametophytic phases in the plant life cycle.

answer.text: Alternation between autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition depending on sunlight
Alternation between plasmodium and fruiting body stages
Alternation between dikaryophase and coenocytic mycelium
Alternation between the diploid sporophytic phase and the haploid gametophytic phase

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q41 - Characteristics of Kingdom Animalia

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets of characteristics accurately defines Kingdom Animalia?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kingdom Animalia comprises multicellular heterotrophic eukaryotes with distinct structural and nutritional features.

Step 2: Evaluation
Members of Kingdom Animalia lack cell walls, digest food in an internal cavity, store food reserves as glycogen or fat, and have a holozoic mode of nutrition (by ingestion of food). They also follow a definite growth pattern and grow into adults of definite shape and size.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, multicellularity without cell walls, holozoic nutrition with internal digestion, and food storage as glycogen or fat define Kingdom Animalia.

answer.text: Multicellular eukaryotes lacking cell walls; holozoic nutrition; food stored as glycogen or fat
Unicellular eukaryotes with cellulosic cell walls; photosynthetic nutrition; food stored as starch
Multicellular eukaryotes with chitinous cell walls; saprophytic nutrition; indefinite growth
Multicellular prokaryotes lacking nuclear membrane; chemosynthetic nutrition

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q42 - Nature of viruses outside and inside host cells

questiontext.text: Why did viruses not find a place in Whittaker's five-kingdom classification, and what is their state outside a living cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Living organisms in the five-kingdom classification are defined by having a cellular structure.

Step 2: Evaluation
Viruses are non-cellular organisms that are characterised by having an inert crystalline structure outside the living cell. Because they lack a cell structure, they are not considered truly 'living'. Once they infect a host cell, they take over its machinery to replicate themselves and are obligate parasites.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, viruses are non-cellular and exist as an inert crystalline structure outside a living cell.

answer.text: They are prokaryotic cells; they actively divide by binary fission outside host cells
They are non-cellular organisms; they have an inert crystalline structure outside the living cell
They are unicellular eukaryotes; they form a plasmodium outside host cells
They are symbiotic associations; they grow only in polluted areas

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q43 - Contributions of Ivanowsky, Beijerinek, and Stanley

questiontext.text: Who demonstrated that the extract of infected tobacco plants could cause infection in healthy plants and called the fluid Contagium vivum fluidum?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The discovery and characterisation of viruses unfolded through key experiments on tobacco mosaic disease.

Step 2: Evaluation
Dmitri Ivanowsky (1892) recognised microbes smaller than bacteria causing mosaic disease of tobacco that passed through bacteria-proof filters. M.W. Beijerinek (1898) demonstrated that the extract of infected tobacco plants could infect healthy plants and called the fluid Contagium vivum fluidum (infectious living fluid). W.M. Stanley (1935) later showed that viruses could be crystallised.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, M.W. Beijerinek (1898) named the infectious extract Contagium vivum fluidum.

answer.text: Dmitri Ivanowsky (1892)
W.M. Stanley (1935)
M.W. Beijerinek (1898)
T.O. Diener (1971)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q44 - Genetic material in plant, animal, and bacterial viruses

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately describes the genetic material of viruses?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A virus is a nucleoprotein whose genetic material is infectious.

Step 2: Evaluation
No virus contains both RNA and DNA. In general, viruses that infect plants have single-stranded RNA, viruses that infect animals have either single- or double-stranded RNA or double-stranded DNA, and bacterial viruses (bacteriophages) are usually double-stranded DNA viruses.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, no virus contains both RNA and DNA; plant viruses generally have single-stranded RNA, and bacteriophages usually have double-stranded DNA.

answer.text: Every virus contains both RNA and DNA simultaneously
Plant viruses generally have double-stranded DNA, whereas bacteriophages have single-stranded RNA
Animal viruses contain only single-stranded RNA and never DNA
No virus contains both RNA and DNA; plant viruses generally have single-stranded RNA and bacteriophages usually have double-stranded DNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q45 - Viral capsid structure and plant viral symptoms

questiontext.text: What is the protein coat of a virus called, what subunits is it made of, and what symptoms do viruses cause in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Viruses protect their infectious nucleic acid with a geometric protein shell and induce characteristic symptoms in infected hosts.

Step 2: Evaluation
The protein coat is called the capsid, made of small subunits called capsomeres arranged in helical or polyhedral geometric forms. In plants, viral symptoms include mosaic formation, leaf rolling and curling, yellowing and vein clearing, dwarfing, and stunted growth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the coat is the capsid made of capsomeres, and plant viral symptoms include mosaic formation, leaf rolling and curling, yellowing and vein clearing, dwarfing, and stunted growth.

answer.text: Capsid made of capsomeres; mosaic formation, leaf rolling and curling, yellowing and vein clearing, dwarfing, and stunted growth
Pellicle made of chitin; white spots on mustard leaves and wheat rust
Sheath made of cellulose; citrus canker and potato spindle tuber
Ascocarp made of hyphae; red tides and sleeping sickness

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q46 - Viroids discovery, structure, and disease

questiontext.text: How do viroids (discovered by T.O. Diener in 1971) differ from viruses, and which disease do they cause?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Viroids are sub-viral infectious agents that are structurally simpler than viruses.

Step 2: Evaluation
Discovered by T.O. Diener in 1971, viroids are smaller than viruses, consist of free RNA of low molecular weight, and lack the protein coat (capsid) found in viruses. They cause potato spindle tuber disease.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, viroids are smaller than viruses, consist of low molecular weight free RNA without a protein coat, and cause potato spindle tuber disease.

answer.text: Viroids consist of abnormally folded protein without RNA and cause mad cow disease
Viroids consist of free low molecular weight RNA lacking a protein coat and cause potato spindle tuber disease
Viroids contain double-stranded DNA inside a polyhedral capsid and cause tobacco mosaic disease
Viroids are larger than bacteria and cause citrus canker

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q47 - Prions and neurological diseases

questiontext.text: What is the chemical nature of prions, and which notable diseases do they cause in cattle and humans?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain infectious neurological diseases are transmitted by proteinaceous agents lacking nucleic acids.

Step 2: Evaluation
Prions are infectious agents similar in size to viruses that consist of abnormally folded protein. The most notable diseases caused by prions are bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), commonly called mad cow disease in cattle, and its analogous variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) in humans.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, prions consist of abnormally folded protein and cause BSE (mad cow disease) in cattle and CJD in humans.

answer.text: Free low molecular weight RNA; potato spindle tuber disease and tobacco mosaic disease
Double-stranded DNA with a capsid; mumps and smallpox
Abnormally folded protein; bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) in cattle and Cr–Jacob disease (CJD) in humans
Nucleoprotein complexes; sleeping sickness and malaria

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOLOGICALCLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q48 - Lichens phycobiont, mycobiont, and pollution indicators

questiontext.text: In lichens, what are the roles of the phycobiont and mycobiont, and why are lichens considered very good pollution indicators?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Lichens are mutually useful symbiotic associations between algae and fungi.

Step 2: Evaluation
The algal component is the phycobiont (autotrophic), which prepares food for the fungi. The fungal component is the mycobiont (heterotrophic), which provides shelter and absorbs mineral nutrients and water for its partner. Lichens are very good pollution indicators because they do not grow in polluted areas.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the autotrophic phycobiont prepares food while the heterotrophic mycobiont provides shelter and absorbs minerals and water, and lichens do not grow in polluted areas.

answer.text: Phycobiont is fungal and absorbs minerals; mycobiont is algal and prepares food; they flourish in polluted areas
Phycobiont is heterotrophic and provides shelter; mycobiont is autotrophic and fixes nitrogen; they indicate water blooms
Both partners are parasitic on higher plant roots; they grow rapidly in industrial smoke
Phycobiont (algal, autotrophic) prepares food and mycobiont (fungal, heterotrophic) provides shelter and absorbs minerals and water; they do not grow in polluted areas
